body.p: Claims 1-20 are pending with claims 1, 6, 8, 13, 15, 16, and 20 having been amended. Support for the amended claims can be found in FIG. 1C and corresponding paragraphs of the Application as filed.

Claims 1-20 were rejected under 35 U.S.C.101 as being directed to a judicial exception without significantly more. Claims 8-20 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) as being indefinite. Claims 1-20 were rejected under 102(a)(1) as being anticipated by Umezawa (U.S. Patent Pub. No. 20 17/0055842).

Applicant-initiated telephone interview summary. Applicant thanks Examiner Chu Chuan Liu for the courtesies and thoughtful treatment afforded to Applicant's representative, Rahjima Francia (Reg. No. 76,812), during the telephonic interview conducted on November 18,2024. During the interview, the disclosure, a proposed amendment, and the rejections in the Office Action were discussed. No agreement was reached regarding the patentability of the claims, but the Examiner indicated that Applicant's arguments would be subject to further search and consideration.
A. Claims 1-19 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 as directed to non-statutory
subject matter. This rejection is respectfully overcome.

Without acquiescing to the propriety of the rejection and solely in an effort to advance prosecution, Applicant has amended claim 1 consistent with the Examiner's suggestion to include additional structures from FIG. 1 C as discussed in the interview. Accordingly, Applicant respectfully requests that the rejections to claim 1, (and claims 2-7 which depend from claim 1), and corresponding claims 8-20 be withdrawn.

Applicant respectfully submits that claim 1 is not directed to an abstract idea. However, even assuming arguendo that claim 1 includes an abstract idea articulated in the Office Action, claim 1 integrates the alleged abstract idea into a practical application under Step 2A, Prong 2 or is directed to substantially more than a judicial exception under Step 2B.

Applicant submits that claim 1 provides improved performance for accurately measuring a physiological characteristic using a multi-channel optical sensor. Claim 1, as amended, includes a specific structure that includes an optical sensor having a plurality of channels, a plurality of light detectors, and a plurality of light emitters, wherein each of the plurality of channels of the optical sensor correspond to at least one of the plurality of emitters and at least one of the plurality of light detectors. Claim 1 further recites a specific manner of detecting spatially localized measurement inconsistency and to mitigate or reduce its effect to improve the accuracy of the estimate of a physiological characteristic. In particular, claim 1 requires estimating a multi-dimensional representation of physiological characteristics in tissue using physiological characteristics computed from measurements of a plurality of channels of the optical sensor; processing the multi-dimensional representation; determining that the multi- dimensional representation includes a region that meets one or more criteria indicative of a spatially localized measurement inconsistency; and in response to the determination that the multi-dimensional representation includes the region that meets the one or more criteria indicative of a spatially localized measurement inconsistency, computing an estimated physiological characteristic from the multi-dimensional representation excluding the region. Thus, rather than describing, as alleged by the Office Action, "a claim whose entire scope can be performed mentally" and "merely covering the collection of data obtained from known and existing technology and processing/analyzing the data" (see page 3 of the Office Action),

amended claim 1 recites a practical application and improved implementation of the alleged abstract idea by providing improved accuracy of SpO2 measurement with operations to generate a 3D representation of the physiological characteristic based on input parameters including the cSpO2 values for the multiple channels of the optical sensor; and processing the 3D representation to detect and mitigate spatially localized tissue anomalies that cause errors with pulse oximetry at the wrist using information about the cSpO2 values from the multiple channels. This is an important improvement because as stated in paragraph [0020] reproduced below:
"In some examples, inconsistent measurement of the physiological
characteristic (e.g., SpO2) may occur (e.g., relative to a user's true SpO2) despite the underlying physiological signals (e.g., photoplethysmogram signals measured
using an optical sensor) having quality characteristics consistent with
physiologically valid signals showing a consistent cardiac signal indicative of
accurate measurement of the physiological characteristic. In particular, the
measurement inconsistency may be associated with a spatially localized region
(e.g., corresponding to some measurement channel(s) of an electronic device
and/or the underlying tissue measured by the channel(s)), referred to herein as a
spatially localized measurement inconsistency. Such measurement inconsistency may result in an incorrect, low estimate of the physiological characteristic relative
to the true characteristic (e.g., an SpO2 estimate may skew lower than the true
SpO2). Thus, spatially localized measurement inconsistency can make accurate
estimation of SpO2 difficult, especially measurements at certain areas of the body
(e.g., at the wrist)."
Claim 1 recites the detection and mitigation of spatially localized measurement

inconsistencies and thereby reduces their effects to improve the accuracy of the estimate of the physiological characteristic. Furthermore, claim 1 as a whole also integrates such detection and mitigation processes into a practical application that can provide accurate estimation of SpO2, which can be difficult, at certain areas of the body, such as the wrist. The claims thus integrate the alleged abstract idea into a practical application.
Because claim 1 includes additional structures, such as a plurality of emitters and a

plurality of light detectors operable for emitting/detecting light at multiple wavelengths in the plurality of channels of the optical sensor, wherein measurements of the plurality of channels of the optical sensor are used in generating a multi-dimensional representation for detecting spatially localized measurement inconsistencies as described herein that are integrated into a practical application, claim 1 is not directed to an abstract idea such that the rejection under 35

U.S.C. § 101 is overcome on this basis. In this regard, the Guidance states that "If the recited exception is integrated into a practical application of the exception, then the claim is eligible at Prong Two of revised Step 2A. This concludes the eligibility analysis."

For each of the foregoing reasons, claim 1, is not directed to an abstract idea such that the rejection under 35 USC § 101 is overcome on this basis. Accordingly, Applicant respectfully requests reconsideration and withdrawal of the rejection of claim 1 under 35 U.S.C. § 101. Claims 2-20 are dependent from independent claim 1 and/or include similar recitations such that the rejection of claims 2-20 under 35 USC § 101 are also overcome.
B. Claims 8-20 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) as being indefinite. This
rejection is respectfully overcome.

Specifically, claims 8 and 15 were both rejected for reciting claims limitations without sufficient antecedent basis. As presently amended, claims 8 and 15 have been amended to provide sufficient antecedent basis. In view of the amendments to claims 8 and 15, Applicant respectfully requests that the rejections under§ 112(b) be withdrawn.
C. Claims 1-20 were rejected under 102(a)(1) as being anticipated by Umezawa.
This rejection is respectfully traversed.

Umezawa does not disclose "computing an estimated physiological characteristic from the multi-dimensional representation excluding the region" in response to "a determination that the multi-dimensional representation includes a region that meets one or more criteria indicative of a spatially localized measurement inconsistency," as required by claim 1. Umezawa relates to photoacoustic imaging. In particular, Umezawa emits light into an object (e.g., organ, bone, muscle, etc.) to generate photoacoustic waves that are converted to electrical signals. These signals are analyzed to extract information about the object. The information extracted enables detection and analysis of specific features, such as blood vessels, tumors, and blood oxygen saturation.
In FIG. 3 (reproduced below), and corresponding paragraphs, Umezawa discloses
identifying a region of interest (ROI) by detecting regions with high absorption coefficients, and applying a mask within the ROI to identify blood vessels. In FIG. 3 below, image 101 represents
the complete absorption coefficient distribution across a scanned area. Mask 102 highlights the blood vessel within a defined ROI.

Umezawa discloses calculating a representative value (e.g., mean, media, or mode) for data within the mask. This value replaces the data in the mask to avoid noise influence. Umezawa further discloses that a final distribution of absorption coefficients is calculated based on the processed mask (e.g., substituted with the representative value) and the unmasked data. However, Umezawa does not "compute an estimated physiological characteristic from the multi- dimensional representation excluding the region" (emphasis added). Instead, Umezawa enhances the data within the mask (e.g., substitutes the data with representative values) and uses original data outside of the mask. The union of enhanced data within the mask and original data outside of the mask cannot be equated with "excluding the region." Thus, this substitution cannot reasonably be interpreted to relate to "computing an estimated physiological characteristic from the multi-dimensional representation excluding the region" in response to "a determination that the multi-dimensional representation includes a region that meets one or more criteria indicative of a spatially localized measurement inconsistency," as required by claim 1.
As such, Umezawa fails to teach or suggest that which is recited by claim 1 such that

Umezawa cannot anticipate claim 1. Independent claims 8 and 15 while having their own scope, recite features similar to those of independent claim 1, such that claims 8 and 15 are similarly not anticipated by Umezawa.

Because each of the dependent claims includes each of the recitations of a respective independent base claim, Applicant further submits that the dependent claims are patentably distinct from the cited references, taken alone or in combination, for at least those reasons as discussed above. Accordingly, Applicant respectfully submits that the rejections of the dependent claims are overcome and the dependent claims are in condition for allowance. As the patentability of the independent claims has been argued as set forth above, Applicant will not take this opportunity to argue the merits of the rejection with regard to specific dependent claims. However, Applicant does not concede that the dependent claims are not independently patentable and reserves the right to argue the patentability of dependent claims at a later date if necessary.

By responding in the foregoing remarks only to particular positions asserted by the Examiner, Applicant does not necessarily acquiesce in other positions that have not been explicitly addressed. In addition, Applicant's arguments for the patentability of a claim should not be understood as implying that no other reasons for the patentability of that claim exist.
In view of the above, each of the presently pending claims in this application is

believed to be in immediate condition for allowance. Accordingly, the Examiner is respectfully requested to withdraw the outstanding rejection of the claims and to pass this application to issue.
